section_summary: This section concludes a confidential study arguing that Japan’s economic strain, strategic-material shortages, and political divisions could encourage further aggression toward the Dutch East Indies, while warning that a U.S. embargo might precipitate war. It then documents commodity shortages, inflation, price-control evasion, industrial expansion, foreign trade, and financial weakness during 1939–1940. The final documents examine Japanese plans for an economically self-sufficient Japan–Manchukuo–China bloc and debate whether the plans represented new realism or merely reinforced Japan’s existing exploitation of occupied China.

subfiles.title: Confidential study of Japan’s economic position and measures short of war, concluding sections
subfiles.from: 2nd Lt. Norman E. Towson, Military Intelligence Reserve
subfiles.about: The concluding sections connect Japan’s economic weakness with political instability, possible southward aggression, and the consequences of an American embargo.
subfiles.summary: The study describes divisions among Japanese moderates, Army extremists, business interests, and advocates of continuing the war in China. It reviews Japan’s dependence on American strategic materials and warns that a total embargo might eliminate restraints on Japanese aggression and force a choice between retreat and armed conflict. Its conclusion predicts that shortages—especially oil—and dwindling foreign exchange could prompt a move toward the Dutch East Indies, while financial sanctions and embargoes would risk Japanese military retaliation.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on FBI-supplied documents concerning Japanese political groupings
subfiles.about: The memorandum evaluates documents sent by the FBI and recommends no further reply.
subfiles.summary: The writer notes that an identical document had accompanied Peiping despatch no. 2236 of August 31, 1939. Most of the material was regarded as common knowledge and neither new nor important. The Division of Far Eastern Affairs recommended that no further communication be sent to the FBI.

subfiles.title: FBI letter transmitting information on political and military groups in Japan
subfiles.from: J. Edgar Hoover, Director, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.to: Adolf A. Berle Jr., Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Hoover transmits photostatic documents describing political factions, Army divisions, and economic regimentation in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The letter says that a Chinese observer recently returned from Tokyo had identified pro-democratic, pro-Axis, and neutral groups and divisions among Japanese Army leaders. An accompanying assessment argues that military extremists sought totalitarian control of national resources to sustain warfare, while opposition was growing among groups defending private interests and rights. Copies were also supplied to naval and military intelligence officials.

subfiles.title: Differences of opinion on foreign policies and among Army leaders
subfiles.about: The enclosure classifies Japanese civilian and military leaders by their foreign-policy alignments and Army factions.
subfiles.summary: Civilian figures are divided into pro-democratic, pro-Axis, and neutral groups, with roles and institutional connections listed. Army officers are arranged into competing factions, including the relatively conservative Control Faction, an expansionist group associated with the Kwantung Army and Manchukuo, and the Araki–Masaki tendency connected with the February 26 revolt. The commentary also identifies the senior Army offices believed to control national military policy.

subfiles.title: Duplicate copy of “Differences of opinion on foreign policies and among Army leaders”
subfiles.about: This is a second, more poorly reproduced copy of the political and Army faction analysis on pages 87–90.
subfiles.summary: The duplicate again lists civilian leaders as pro-democratic, pro-Axis, or neutral and groups Army officers by faction. Its explanatory section contrasts conservative central control with the expansionist officers linked to the Mukden Incident and Manchukuo. Severe OCR degradation obscures several names and titles, but the substance matches the preceding enclosure.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of FBI letter concerning economic conditions in Japan
subfiles.from: Adolf A. Berle Jr., Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.to: J. Edgar Hoover, Director, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.about: Berle acknowledges receipt of the FBI’s photostatic documents and thanks Hoover for sending them.
subfiles.summary: The reply confirms receipt of Hoover’s March 18 letter and its documents concerning Japanese economic conditions. It also notes that the information had been furnished to Rear Admiral Walter S. Anderson and Colonel E. R. Warner McCabe. Berle closes with a brief expression of appreciation.

subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs abstract of Tokyo despatch no. 4556
subfiles.about: The abstract summarizes Ambassador Grew’s report on shortages, price-control evasion, and Japan’s expanded productive capacity.
subfiles.summary: It states that serious shortages of basic commodities and daily necessities had produced widespread and intricate evasions of price controls. Although factual economic information was difficult to obtain, the Embassy believed that Japan’s productive mechanism had expanded during the preceding two years. Those facilities, it observed, would survive even an economic collapse.

subfiles.title: Growing Shortages in Basic Commodities and Daily Necessities
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The despatch analyzes shortages, inflation, price-control evasion, and the effects of Japan’s war-oriented industrial policy.
subfiles.summary: Grew attributes the lack of consumer goods to military production, state-sponsored heavy-industry expansion, rising money circulation, and rigid price controls. He describes fourteen methods used to evade official prices and reviews proposals for subsidies, rationing, savings promotion, and direct state control of essential commodities. Reliable statistics were scarce, but shortages, hoarding, illegal trade, and rising living costs were unmistakable. Grew nevertheless stresses that Japan had substantially expanded its productive facilities, which would remain even after an inflationary or deflationary collapse.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs note on Department of Commerce study
subfiles.about: A handwritten note evaluates and routes the Department of Commerce study “Economic Situation in Japan in 1939.”
subfiles.summary: The note says the attached study was based largely on commercial attaché reports, especially the annual report. Although it contained little that was new to the Division of Far Eastern Affairs, the reviewer found it useful and worthwhile. Two extra copies were attached.

subfiles.title: Newspaper clipping on Japan’s 1939 economy and adjacent news items
subfiles.about: The clipping summarizes a government report on Japan’s weakened economy and includes adjacent items about Luxembourg’s diplomatic representation and an art sale for Chinese relief.
subfiles.summary: The principal article reports inflation, commodity shortages, debt growth, labor inefficiency, and limited industrial gains despite expanding heavy industry. It notes improved rural prosperity and stronger Japanese trade with the United States, while emphasizing that much export growth went to Manchuria and China without earning foreign exchange. Adjacent columns report Hughes Le Gallais’s reception as Luxembourg chargé d’affaires and a charity art sale sponsored by the American Bureau for Medical Aid for China.

subfiles.title: Economic Situation in Japan in 1939
subfiles.from: Bureau of Foreign and Domestic Commerce, Department of Commerce
subfiles.about: The report surveys Japanese industry, agriculture, labor, prices, public finance, exchange control, and trade during 1939.
subfiles.summary: Japan’s wartime economy showed high activity but mounting weakness: inflation, debt, taxes, commodity shortages, labor problems, and declining operating efficiency. Heavy industry expanded while consumer production suffered, and price controls failed to prevent sharp increases in living costs. Agriculture and rural incomes improved, although urban rice shortages persisted, while silk prices rose dramatically. Foreign trade reached record nominal levels, but much of the increase involved the yen bloc and produced little usable foreign exchange; Japan consequently remained dependent on the United States for key materials.

subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs abstract of Tokyo despatch no. 4801
subfiles.about: The abstract summarizes the effects of the European war on Japanese foreign trade.
subfiles.summary: The war disrupted the triangular trade linking Germany, Japan, and Manchuria and cut off machinery, pulp, steel, bearings, and other industrial supplies. Japanese exports had neither greatly benefited nor suffered, and most 1940 growth was in yen-bloc markets. The result was increased Japanese dependence on the American market and a stronger emphasis on securing sources of supply.

subfiles.title: Effect of European War on Japan’s Foreign Trade
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Grew compares the European war’s effects on Japanese trade with Japan’s boom during the First World War.
subfiles.summary: Unlike 1914–1918, the new war initially offered Japan few major export opportunities because China absorbed military resources and much Far Eastern trade yielded only paper yen. Loss of German and European machinery and raw-material supplies damaged industrial expansion and increased dependence on the United States for machinery, cotton, petroleum, scrap iron, copper, chemicals, wheat, and pulp. Japanese exports remained relatively stable, but wartime controls threatened future markets. Trade agreements with the Netherlands Indies, Uruguay, Thailand, Nicaragua, Colombia, and prospective partners were intended chiefly to secure essential imports.

subfiles.title: Telegram 476 requesting verification of Japanese economic-development plans
subfiles.to: American Embassies at Tokyo and Peiping; repeated to Shanghai
subfiles.about: The Department asks the embassies to investigate reported ten-year and five-year plans for economic development in Japan, Manchukuo, and North China.
subfiles.summary: Press reports described a ten-year scheme assigning skilled industry to Japan, agricultural production and colonization to Manchukuo, and unskilled labor and resource development to China. A separate five-year North China plan appeared to emphasize coal, agriculture, and repair of existing railways rather than grandiose new construction. The Department wondered whether these reports indicated greater realism or a policy shift and requested prompt verification and continuing reports.

subfiles.title: Tokyo telegram 1175 on the ten-year Japan–Manchukuo–China economic plan
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The Embassy reports the officially published outline of a ten-year plan for a self-sufficient Greater East Asian economic sphere.
subfiles.summary: The Cabinet Information Bureau called for an economy that was “higher, wider and stronger” and minimally dependent on countries outside Greater East Asia. Japan was assigned precision manufacturing and heavy industry, Manchukuo mining, electricity, food production, and Japanese settlement, and China raw-material production and later industrial development. The plan also envisioned labor transfers, trained technicians, coordinated finance, nonconvertible-yen settlements, and integrated transportation and communications. A related North China program sought sharply increased coal production, agricultural self-sufficiency, light industry, Japanese capital, and labor supplies for Manchukuo.

subfiles.title: Peiping telegram 473 on publicity and commentary concerning the ten-year plan
subfiles.about: The telegram reports local descriptions and competing assessments of Japan’s ten-year yen-bloc development program.
subfiles.summary: Japanese reports envisioned joint operation of the economies of Japan, Manchukuo, and China, transfer of Japanese light industry to the continent, and specialization in machinery, raw materials, agriculture, and textiles. The Peking Chronicle presented the plan favorably, while Shingo Tsuda claimed synthetic fuels, low-grade ores, hemp, and chemical fibers would soon free Japan from foreign petroleum, iron, cotton, and wool. Shanghai’s Finance and Commerce judged the scheme vulnerable because it ignored Chinese opposition and assumed cooperation before China had been conquered.

subfiles.title: Peiping telegram 486 on North China’s five-year development plan
subfiles.about: The telegram traces the reported five-year North China plan to an article in the Japanese-controlled Chen Pao.
subfiles.summary: The plan was intended to make North China more self-sufficient and increase coal supplies for Japan, Manchukuo, and Central China. Measures included expanding cotton production through irrigation and land reclamation, using hydroelectric power in mining, and improving railways. Harbor improvements were proposed at Qingdao and Tanggu, with a new harbor at Qinhuangdao.

subfiles.title: Duplicate copy of Peiping telegram 486
subfiles.about: This duplicate repeats the Embassy’s account of the Chen Pao article on North China’s five-year development plan.
subfiles.summary: The telegram again identifies self-sufficiency and greater coal output as the plan’s main purposes. It lists irrigation, land reclamation, hydroelectric power, railway repair and construction, and harbor improvements. Copies were sent to Chongqing and Shanghai and forwarded by mail to Tianjin and Tokyo.

subfiles.title: Peiping telegram 489 rejecting the interpretation of a Japanese policy shift
subfiles.about: The Embassy argues that the new development plans reinforce rather than moderate Japan’s existing economic policy in occupied China.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy found no evidence that Japanese planners had recognized earlier schemes as overly optimistic, notwithstanding failures in implementation. Minor regulatory adjustments and occasional promises of better treatment had not removed the principal restrictions on normal economic development in occupied areas. The continuing movement was toward full state control for Japan’s benefit, so the ten-year yen-bloc program and North China five-year plan were interpreted as reaffirmations of existing policy rather than signs of realism.
